source.title: Pine Ridge Agency | Indian Affairs
source.publisher: U.S. Department of the Interior, Bureau of Indian Affairs

nations.name: Omaha Tribe of Nebraska
nations.lands: Omaha Reservation, Nebraska, United States; tribal offices in Macy

facts.text: The Omaha Tribe of Nebraska holds a trust land base of 27,828 acres, according to the Bureau of Indian Affairs.

source.title: Winnebago Agency | Indian Affairs
source.publisher: U.S. Department of the Interior, Bureau of Indian Affairs

facts.text: The Bureau of Indian Affairs estimates enrollment in the Omaha Tribe of Nebraska at 5,427 members.

source.title: Winnebago Agency | Indian Affairs
source.publisher: U.S. Department of the Interior, Bureau of Indian Affairs

nations.name: Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe
nations.lands: Three districts in East Central Minnesota, United States

facts.text: The Mille Lacs Band governs itself through a three-branch government that divides power among executive, legislative and judicial branches.

source.title: Welcome | Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe

facts.text: The Mille Lacs Band is a self-governing nation of nearly 4,800 enrolled members, with homelands in three districts of East Central Minnesota.

source.title: Welcome | Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe

nations.name: Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians
nations.lands: Rolette County, North Dakota, near the Canadian border, United States

facts.text: Members of the Turtle Mountain Band speak English, Ojibwe and Michif, a language that blends French, Ojibwe and Cree.

source.title: Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa | Indian Affairs Commission, North Dakota

facts.text: As of July 2024, an estimated 33,276 members were enrolled in the Turtle Mountain Band.

source.title: Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa | Indian Affairs Commission, North Dakota

nations.name: Absentee Shawnee Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma
nations.lands: central Oklahoma, including the Shawnee and Little Axe areas

facts.text: The Tribe's government page describes separate Legislative/Executive and Judicial branches, alongside an independent Election Commission.

source.title: Government | Absentee Shawnee Tribe
source.publisher: Absentee Shawnee Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma

facts.text: The Tribe's language page lists a lexicon and online lessons among its resources; the index does not establish access conditions or teaching availability.

source.title: Language | Absentee Shawnee Tribe
source.publisher: Absentee Shawnee Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma

nations.name: Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians
nations.lands: Eastern Upper Peninsula of Michigan, United States

facts.text: Sault Tribe serves seven eastern Upper Peninsula counties: Chippewa, Luce, Mackinac, Schoolcraft, Alger, Delta and Marquette.

source.title: About Us - The Sault Tribe of Chippewa Indians Official Web Site
source.publisher: Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians

facts.text: Sault Tribe is a federally recognized tribe of about 44,000 members.

source.title: About Us - The Sault Tribe of Chippewa Indians Official Web Site
source.publisher: Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians

nations.name: Iowa Tribe of Oklahoma
nations.lands: Central Oklahoma, United States; centered in Perkins

facts.text: The Iowa Tribe of Oklahoma is a sovereign nation centered in Perkins, Oklahoma, with self-government recognized by treaties and legislation.
The Iowa people's own name, Baxoje, means People of the Grey Snow.

pronounce.text: Baxoje, the people's own name: Bah Kho-je
pronounce.publisher: Iowa Tribe of Oklahoma, on its own site

nations.name: Syilx Okanagan Nation
nations.lands: The Okanagan, Similkameen and Nicola areas of British Columbia, Canada, and northern Washington State, United States

facts.text: Historically the Okanagan Nation Alliance represented eight member communities: seven in Canada and the Colville Confederated Tribes in Washington State.
The Okanagan Nation Alliance reports that the new Okanagan Dam Fish Passage, after years of advocacy and planning, lets salmon reach Okanagan Lake for the first time in nearly 100 years.

nations.name: Kahnawà:ke
nations.lands: On the south shore of the St. Lawrence River, near Montreal, Quebec, Canada

facts.text: For more than a hundred years, many people from Kahnawà:ke, mostly men, have worked in the ironworking trade, much of it in the United States.
About 8,000 people live in Kahnawà:ke, on the banks of the St. Lawrence River about 10 kilometres south of Montreal.

nations.name: Nunavik Inuit
nations.lands: Nunavik, northern Quebec, Canada: 15 villages along Hudson Bay, Hudson Strait and Ungava Bay

facts.text: Makivvik, an Inuktitut name meaning 'to rise up', protects Nunavik Inuit rights under the 1975 James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement, Canada's first comprehensive Inuit land claim.
Language retention among Nunavik Inuit is over 95 percent, and Inuktitut remains the main language spoken in the region.

nations.name: Inuit of Nunavut
nations.lands: Nunavut, Canada: the Qikiqtaaluk, Kivalliq and Kitikmeot regions

facts.text: Nunavut became Canada's newest territory on April 1, 1999, and Inuktitut is an official language of its government with Inuinnaqtun, English and French.
Under the agreement Inuit own about 350,000 square kilometres of land, including about 35,000 square kilometres with mineral rights.

nations.name: Wolastoqiyik
nations.lands: The Wolastoq (Saint John River) watershed, from the Bay of Fundy to the St. Lawrence: New Brunswick and Quebec in Canada, and Maine in the United States

facts.text: Six Wolastoqey communities in New Brunswick, Matawaskiye, Neqotkuk, Pilick, Sitansisk, Welamukotuk and Wotstak, work together through the Wolastoqey Nation in New Brunswick.
The Wolastoqiyik are the people of the Wolastoq watershed, a homeland of land, sea and fresh water reaching from the Bay of Fundy to the St. Lawrence River.

nations.name: Siksika Nation
nations.lands: East of Calgary, Alberta, Canada; part of the Blackfoot Confederacy

facts.text: Siksika's coat of arms, registered with the Canadian Heraldic Authority in June 1992, was the first registered by any Nation in Canada.
Siksika Nation has about 7,800 members, and its language is Siksika, or Blackfoot.

nations.name: Nuu-chah-nulth
nations.lands: The west coast of Vancouver Island, British Columbia, Canada

facts.text: The Nuu-chah-nulth Tribal Council serves fourteen Nuu-chah-nulth First Nations with about 10,000 members, grouped in three regions.
The Council's vision is self-government that builds strong, healthy Nuu-chah-nulth communities.

nations.name: Inuit
nations.lands: Inuit Nunangat: the Inuvialuit Settlement Region, Nunavut, Nunavik and Nunatsiavut in Arctic Canada

facts.text: Roughly 60 percent of Inuit can hold a conversation in Inuktut, the Inuit language.
Most Inuit in Canada live in 51 communities across Inuit Nunangat, a homeland covering about 40 percent of Canada's land and 72 percent of its coastline.

nations.name: xʷməθkʷəy̓əm
nations.lands: The Fraser River estuary, including much of Metro Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada

facts.text: Musqueam is a strong, growing community of more than 1,300 members, many living on the Musqueam reserve near the mouth of the Fraser River.
The name xʷməθkʷəy̓əm means place of the məθkʷəy̓, a plant, and Musqueam people are traditionally hən̓q̓əmin̓əm̓ speakers.

nations.name: Anishinabek Nation
nations.lands: 39 First Nations across Ontario, Canada, from Pikwàkanagàn in the east and Aamjiwnaang in the south to Lake Nipigon in the north

facts.text: It is Ontario's oldest political organization, with roots in the Confederacy of Three Fires that long predates European contact.
The Anishinabek Nation speaks for 39 First Nations in Ontario with about 70,000 citizens, roughly one third of the province's First Nation population.

nations.name: Dene
nations.lands: Denendeh, the western Northwest Territories, Canada

facts.text: The Dene Nation brings together five regional groups, the Gwich'in, Sahtú, Deh Cho, Tłı̨chǫ and Akaitcho Dene, each with its own language and territory.
Dene simply means 'the people'. Their homeland, Denendeh, lies in the western Northwest Territories.

nations.name: Labrador Inuit
nations.lands: Nunatsiavut, on the north coast of Labrador, Canada

facts.text: Nunatsiavut's legislative capital is Hopedale and its administrative capital is Nain.
The Nunatsiavut Government, the self-government of Labrador Inuit, officially came into being on December 1, 2005.

nations.name: Nisg̱a’a Nation
nations.lands: The Nass River Valley (K’alii-Aksim-Lisims) in northwestern British Columbia, Canada

facts.text: The Nisg̱a’a, People of the Nass River, are a self-governing First Nation on Canada's Pacific Coast.
The Nisg̱a’a Final Agreement was the first modern treaty in British Columbia, and it recognizes both Nisg̱a’a Lands and the Nisg̱a’a Government.

nations.name: Métis Nation
nations.lands: The Métis Nation Homeland as described by the Métis National Council: Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, plus parts of Ontario, British Columbia, the Northwest Territories and the northern United States

facts.text: Many historic Métis communities still stand along rivers and lakes once tied to fur trade posts, and many Métis citizens live in cities within the Homeland.
The Métis emerged as a distinct Indigenous people with their own culture, traditions, nationhood and language, Michif.

nations.name: Ktunaxa
nations.lands: ʔamakʔis Ktunaxa: the Kootenay region of southeastern British Columbia, Canada, with Kootenay Tribes also based today in Montana and Idaho, United States

facts.text: The Ktunaxa Nation Council helps represent the shared interests of four Ktunaxa First Nations within ʔamakʔis Ktunaxa, the Ktunaxa homelands.
ʔamakʔis Ktunaxa, the traditional territory, covers about 70,000 square kilometres in the Kootenay region of southeastern British Columbia.

nations.name: Mi’kmaq
nations.lands: Mi’kma’ki: Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and the Gaspé in Canada, with relatives in Maine, United States

facts.text: Mi'kmaw communities in Nova Scotia wrote their own Netukulimk Livelihood Management Plans so members who fish can support themselves and their families.
In 2006 the 13 Mi'kmaw Chiefs of Nova Scotia formed the Assembly of Nova Scotia Mi'kmaw Chiefs to guide the Nation's negotiators on rights and title.

nations.name: Haida Nation
nations.lands: Haida Gwaii, an archipelago off the north coast of British Columbia, Canada

facts.text: The Council of the Haida Nation works to steward the lands and waters of Haida territories and carry Haida culture and language to future generations.
In April 2024 British Columbia and the Council of the Haida Nation signed the Rising Tide agreement, a first of its kind recognizing Haida Aboriginal title in Haida Gwaii.

source.title: For Immediate Release: Haida Nation, B.C. recognize Haida Aboriginal title, a historic first in Canada

nations.name: Mescalero Apache
nations.lands: South-central New Mexico, US (Mescalero Apache Reservation)

facts.text: Today three peoples, the Mescalero, Lipan and Chiricahua Apache, together make up the Mescalero Apache Tribe on a 463,000 acre reservation.
The Mescalero Apache Tribe owns and runs the Inn of the Mountain Gods Resort and the Ski Apache ski area.

source.title: Official Website of the Mescalero Apache Tribe

nations.name: Jicarilla Apache
nations.lands: North-central New Mexico, US, along the Colorado line and across the Continental Divide (Dulce)

facts.text: The Jicarilla Apache Nation reservation spans more than 879,917 acres in north-central New Mexico, and Dulce is its only community and tribal headquarters.
After 1887 the Jicarilla moved their individual allotments back into tribal ownership, keeping their lands and water rights together.

nations.name: Akimel O’otham
nations.lands: Gila River Indian Community, south of Phoenix, Arizona, US, shared with the Pee Posh (Maricopa)

facts.text: The Akimel O’otham welcomed the Pee Posh (Maricopa) to the Gila River long ago, and the two peoples still share its lands and resources today.
Akimel O’otham basket weaving is in revival, and in 2004 the community dedicated the Huhugam Heritage Center to care for its heritage.

nations.name: Yoreme
nations.lands: Southern Sonora (Etchojoa, Huatabampo, Navojoa) and northern Sinaloa (Ahome, El Fuerte, Guasave), Mexico

facts.text: Yoreme communities have traditional governors. In December 2025 they met Mexico’s federal agrarian office to set a path for continuing the Yoreme-Mayo Justice Plan.

source.title: Atienden Plan de Justicia al pueblo Yoreme-Mayo de Sonora

facts.text: Yoreme patron saint fiestas strengthen the social networks that link communities across Mayo lands and keep Yoreme identity alive.

source.title: Mayos
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

nations.name: Ute Mountain Ute Tribe
nations.lands: Towaoc and reservation lands in southwestern Colorado and northwestern New Mexico; White Mesa, Utah, United States

facts.text: The Ute Mountain Ute Tribe identifies itself as the Weenuche band of the Ute Nation, with its tribal offices in Towaoc, Colorado.
White Mesa Administration supports community members with employment, education and access to basic services in White Mesa, Utah.

nations.name: Comcaac
nations.lands: Desert coast of Sonora on the Gulf of California, Mexico, including Punta Chueca, El Desemboque and Tiburón Island

facts.text: In 1975 Mexico declared the Canal del Infiernillo an exclusive Comcaac fishing zone and symbolically granted them Tiburón Island, a nature reserve, as communal land.

source.title: Seris
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

facts.text: Comcaac artisans weave coritas, baskets made since before Spanish contact. A very large one can take a year or two to finish.

source.title: Seris
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

nations.name: Hualapai
nations.lands: Northwestern Arizona, US, along the Grand Canyon and Colorado River (Peach Springs)

facts.text: The name Hualapai means People of the Tall Pines.
The Hualapai Reservation, set up in 1883, covers about one million acres along 108 miles of the Grand Canyon and Colorado River.

nations.name: Warihó and Macurawe
nations.lands: Foothills of the Sierra Madre Occidental on the Chihuahua and Sonora border, Mexico

facts.text: The people call themselves Macurawe in Sonora and Warihó in Chihuahua. Their Uto-Aztecan language has two variants and bridges Tarahumara and Mayo.

source.title: Guarijíos
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

facts.text: Warihó and Macurawe families weave baskets, mats and hats from palm and fiber and build harps, violins and guitars. Their craft work is family based and rests with women.

source.title: Guarijíos
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

nations.name: Diné
nations.lands: Diné Bikéyah (Navajoland) across Arizona, New Mexico and Utah, US

facts.text: The Navajo Nation Council, the Nation’s governing body, has 24 delegates elected from legislative districts.
Diné Bikéyah, the Navajo Nation, covers more than 27,000 square miles across Arizona, New Mexico and Utah, larger than 10 of the 50 US states.

nations.name: Havasu Baaja
nations.lands: Havasu Canyon in the Grand Canyon, Arizona, US (village of Supai)

facts.text: Supai is so remote that the US Postal Service carries all mail in and out of the canyon by mule train.
The Havasupai reservation was set up in 1880 and greatly enlarged in 1975. It covers 188,077 acres beside the South Rim of the Grand Canyon.

nations.name: White Mountain Apache
nations.lands: White Mountains of east-central Arizona, US (Fort Apache Indian Reservation, Whiteriver)

facts.text: The White Mountain Apache own and run Sunrise, one of the largest ski resorts in the Southwest, and rare Apache trout swim in reservation streams.
White Mountain Apache people live on 1.6 million acres of their ancestral homeland, the Fort Apache Indian Reservation, set aside in 1891.

nations.name: Tonto Apache Tribe
nations.lands: Payson, Gila County, Arizona, United States

facts.text: The Tonto Apache Tribe is based beside Payson in northwestern Gila County, Arizona.
In 2010, land for the Tonto Apache Tribe was acquired in trust following a land exchange with the U.S. Forest Service.

source.title: Reservation proclamation for trust land belonging to the Tonto Apache Tribe of Arizona

nations.name: Yavapai
nations.lands: Central and western Arizona, US, including Fort McDowell near Phoenix and Prescott

facts.text: In September 2026 the Fort McDowell Yavapai Nation, about 950 members, marked 123 years since its land was set aside in 1903.

source.title: Welcome to Fort McDowell Yavapai Nation

facts.text: In 1976 Fort McDowell Yavapai community members voted 144 to 57 against selling their land for the Orme Dam, and in 1981 the dam was called off.

nations.name: Ohkay Owingeh
nations.lands: Where the Rio Grande and Rio Chama meet, northern New Mexico, US

facts.text: Ohkay Owingeh is the headquarters of the Eight Northern Pueblo Tribal Council.
The people have long called their home Ohkay Owingeh, place of the strong people in Tewa, and officially restored that name in place of San Juan, given in 1598.

nations.name: Cocopah
nations.lands: Lower Colorado River and delta: south of Yuma and near Somerton, Arizona, US, and the Mexicali valley of Baja California and San Luis Río Colorado, Sonora, Mexico

facts.text: About 1,000 Cocopah tribal members live and work on or near their reservation south of Yuma, Arizona, which was established in 1917.
Since 2003 the Cucapá of El Mayor, Baja California, and the Cocopah of Somerton, Arizona, have met each year with dances, songs, crafts and food.

source.title: Cucapás
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

nations.name: Nuche
nations.lands: Southwestern Colorado (Ignacio, Towaoc), northeastern Utah (Uintah and Ouray) and nearby New Mexico and Utah lands, US

facts.text: There are three Ute tribes today: the Southern Ute (Mouache and Capote bands), the Ute Mountain Ute (Weenuche band) and the Northern Ute in Utah.
The Ute Mountain Ute Tribe teaches the Ute language to Head Start children ages 2 to 5 and holds evening language classes for adults.

nations.name: Baniwa
nations.lands: Içana river and the Upper Rio Negro in Amazonas, Brazil, and neighboring Colombia and Venezuela

facts.text: The Baniwa speak languages of the Arawak family along the Içana river.
Baniwa communities live where Brazil meets Colombia and Venezuela, along the Içana river in the Upper Rio Negro region.

nations.name: Wapichana
nations.lands: Northeastern Roraima, Brazil, and the South Rupununi in southwestern Guyana

facts.text: In 2012 Wapichan leaders in Guyana presented a community map and land plan titled Thinking Together for those Coming Behind Us.

source.title: Wapichan people in Guyana present territorial map and community proposals to save ancestral forests

facts.text: The Wapichana language is classified in the Arawak language family.

nations.name: Guarani Mbya
nations.lands: Villages across southern and southeastern Brazil, eastern Paraguay, Misiones province in Argentina, and near Montevideo in Uruguay

facts.text: The Comissão Guarani Yvyrupa, founded in 2006, brings together Guarani collectives in six states of southern and southeastern Brazil.
In Guarani, yvyrupa names the structure that holds up the land, recalling free movement across territory before today's borders.

nations.name: Sápara
nations.lands: Rainforest of Pastaza province in the Ecuadorian Amazon, straddling the border with Peru

facts.text: The Sápara live in a part of the Amazon rainforest that straddles Ecuador and Peru.

source.title: Oral heritage and cultural manifestations of the Zápara people

facts.text: Sápara knowledge of the forest shows in their rich vocabulary for plants and animals and in their knowledge of the forest's medicinal plants.

source.title: Oral heritage and cultural manifestations of the Zápara people

nations.name: Kuikuro
nations.lands: Upper Xingu, in the Xingu Indigenous Territory, Mato Grosso, Brazil

facts.text: Kuikuro is a southern Carib language.
Kuikuro remains a living, intact language, used by everyone in all domains except talking with outsiders.

nations.name: Ka'apor
nations.lands: Northern Maranhão, Brazil, in the Alto Turiaçu Indigenous Land

facts.text: Ka'apor communities have had a shared, standard sign language for communicating with deaf members of the community.
Ka'apor is a language of the Tupi-Guarani family.

nations.name: A'uwe
nations.lands: Eastern Mato Grosso, Brazil, in Indigenous lands such as Pimentel Barbosa, Marãiwatsédé, São Marcos and Sangradouro

facts.text: The A'uwe (Xavante) language belongs to the Jê family of the Macro-Jê language stock.
The Xavante numbered about 22,256 people in 2020.

nations.name: Pataxó
nations.lands: Villages in the far south of Bahia and the north of Minas Gerais, Brazil

facts.text: The Pataxó are rebuilding their language, Patxohã, through a major community effort.
Pataxó villages are spread across the far south of Bahia and the north of Minas Gerais.

nations.name: Macuxi
nations.lands: Fields and mountains of northern Roraima, Brazil, between the headwaters of the Branco and Rupununi rivers, extending into Guyana and Venezuela

facts.text: The Conselho Indígena de Roraima, founded in 1990, unites ten peoples including the Macuxi and Wapichana, with 270 of the state's 465 communities as members.
The Macuxi language belongs to the Carib language family.

nations.name: Ashaninka
nations.lands: Upper Juruá region of Acre, Brazil, including the Amônia, Breu and Envira rivers, near the Peruvian border

facts.text: Ashaninka of the Amônia river created their own association, Apiwtxa, in 1991; it was officially registered in 1993.
Ashenĩka, the people's own name, can be translated as my relatives, my folk or my people.

nations.name: Terena
nations.lands: Mato Grosso do Sul, with communities in Mato Grosso and São Paulo, Brazil

facts.text: Farming remains the main productive activity in Terena reserves.
Terena people living in cities are concentrated mainly in Campo Grande, and most of them keep strong ties with their reserves.

nations.name: Tikuna
nations.lands: Along the upper Solimões (Amazon) river in Amazonas, Brazil, and in neighboring Peru and Colombia

facts.text: Tikuna communities are spread across three countries: Brazil, Peru and Colombia.
Tikuna is a tonal language, considered genetically isolated, with a complex sound system and grammar.

nations.name: Shuar
nations.lands: Zamora Chinchipe, Morona Santiago and southern Pastaza provinces in the Ecuadorian Amazon

facts.text: In 2022 the Shuar Aratsim Center approved its own Life Plan after participatory community workshops.

source.title: Territory of the Shuar People
source.publisher: ReVista, Harvard Review of Latin America (David Rockefeller Center for Latin American Studies)

facts.text: The Interprovincial Federation of Shuar Centers (FICSH), founded in 1964, was one of the pioneering Indigenous organizations of the Amazon.

source.title: Territory of the Shuar People
source.publisher: ReVista, Harvard Review of Latin America (David Rockefeller Center for Latin American Studies)

nations.name: Achuar
nations.lands: Northern Loreto in Peru near the Ecuador border, and the neighboring Amazon of Ecuador

facts.text: Peru's Ministry of Culture has registered five interpreters and translators of the Achuar language.

source.title: Achuar | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

facts.text: Achuar is a cross-border language, spoken in both Peru and Ecuador.

source.title: Achuar | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

nations.name: Avá Guarani
nations.lands: Mato Grosso do Sul and Paraná in Brazil, and eastern Paraguay

facts.text: Guarani peoples, the Avá Guarani among them, live across a territory that spans regions of Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay and Argentina.
The Avá Guarani, called Ñandeva in Brazil, have a present-day territory that takes in parts of Mato Grosso do Sul and Paraná.

source.title: Guarani Kaiowá - Povos Indígenas no Brasil

nations.name: Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians
nations.lands: Siletz, on the central Oregon coast; ancestral territory across western Oregon into southwest Washington and northern California

facts.text: After lobbying Congress, the Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians won repeal of federal termination in 1977.
The Tribe's Athabaskan language dictionary, Nuu-wee-ya' (Our words), holds about 12,000 entries, and a Talking Dictionary lets learners hear words spoken aloud.

source.title: Language - Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians

nations.name: Timbisha Shoshone Tribe
nations.lands: Death Valley and surrounding areas of California and Nevada

facts.text: Today the federally recognized Timbisha Shoshone Tribe works to keep its language, traditions and sovereignty strong.

source.title: Timbisha Shoshone Tribe - California and Nevada

facts.text: The Timbisha, part of the larger Western Shoshone people, have lived in Death Valley and its surrounding areas for thousands of years, and their village sits inside Death Valley National Park.

source.title: Timbisha Shoshone Tribe - California and Nevada

nations.name: Cahuilla Band of Indians
nations.lands: Anza area, Riverside County, Southern California

facts.text: The Band describes itself as a sovereign nation that carries its culture forward through strong governance.
Cahuilla traditional territory spans a large area of what are now Riverside and San Diego counties.

pronounce.text: kuh-WEE-eh (written on the Band's site as kəˊwi:e)
pronounce.publisher: Cahuilla Band of Indians, on its own site

nations.name: Washoe Tribe of Nevada and California
nations.lands: Lake Tahoe region and nearby valleys of western Nevada and eastern California

facts.text: Washoe teachers hold language classes for adults and youth four days a week, and immersion classes reach children in the tribe's Head Start.

source.title: Where Wašiw is Spoken: The Washoe Tribe is Passing Its Unique Language On and Up
source.publisher: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian (American Indian magazine)

facts.text: The name Tahoe is thought to come from Da ow ga, the Washoe word for lake.

source.title: Discover History
source.publisher: USDA Forest Service, Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit

nations.name: Viejas Band of Kumeyaay Indians
nations.lands: Viejas Reservation in the mountains east of San Diego, California; the wider Kumeyaay homeland reaches into Baja California, Mexico

facts.text: Viejas extends its community work beyond San Diego to Kumeyaay relatives in Baja California, Mexico.
Viejas government rests on participatory democracy, with tribal officials elected by the general council to four-year terms.

nations.name: Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe
nations.lands: Pyramid Lake and its reservation, about 35 miles northeast of Reno, Nevada

facts.text: The Tribe's Language Program offers community Paiute classes, lessons inside schools and meetings with fluent speakers.
The reservation covers 475,000 acres around Pyramid Lake, which runs about 27 miles long and 11 miles wide.

nations.name: Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde
nations.lands: Grand Ronde, Yamhill County, northwestern Oregon; ancestral ties across western Oregon, northern California and southwest Washington

facts.text: A nine-member Tribal Council, elected by voting members, governs about 5,400 enrolled members of a confederation of over 30 tribes and bands.
Once at risk of disappearing, Chinuk Wawa is growing again and is actively taught and used in Grand Ronde cultural education.

source.title: Chinuk Wawa Language | Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde

nations.name: Nimiipuu
nations.lands: North-central Idaho, with homelands across present-day Idaho, Washington, Oregon and Montana

facts.text: Nimipuutímt, the Nez Perce language, is a core part of Nimiipuu culture.
Headquartered in Lapwai, Idaho, the Nez Perce Reservation spans about 770,000 acres.

nations.name: Lummi Nation
nations.lands: Northernmost coast of Washington State and the waters of Puget Sound, with ancestral lands reaching into southern British Columbia

facts.text: Northwest Indian College, with its main campus on the Lummi Reservation, is the only accredited tribal college serving Washington, Oregon and Idaho.

source.title: About | Northwest Indian College | Accredited Tribal College

facts.text: The Lhaq'temish, the Lummi People, describe themselves as fishers, hunters, gatherers and harvesters of the Puget Sound shores and waters.

nations.name: Karuk Tribe
nations.lands: Klamath River country of northern California, with tribal offices in Happy Camp

facts.text: The Karuk Language Program teaches all ages through community classes, school partnerships and immersion, linking learners with fluent speakers.
The Karuk People's Center in Happy Camp opened in September 2002 and holds a museum, library, basketweaving classroom and the language program office.

nations.name: Confederated Tribes of the Warm Springs
nations.lands: Central Oregon, stretching east from the summit of the Cascade Mountains

facts.text: The Museum at Warm Springs shares the history and culture of the three tribes and welcomes visitors in Ichishkiin, Numu and Kiksht.

source.title: Museum at Warm Springs - Culture. History. In Living Color.

facts.text: In 1937 the Warm Springs, Wasco and Paiute organized as one confederated government under their own constitution and bylaws.

nations.name: Quinault Indian Nation
nations.lands: Southwestern corner of Washington's Olympic Peninsula, between the Olympic Mountains and the Pacific Ocean

facts.text: The Nation has a Taholah Village Relocation Master Plan that includes planning for an upper village, and its Planning Department is updating the plan for 2026.

source.title: Taholah Village Relocation | Quinault Indian Nation, WA

facts.text: The Quinault Language Department works to revitalize the Quinault language, with in-person classes in Taholah, Queets and Hoquiam.

source.title: Language Department | Quinault Indian Nation, WA

nations.name: Tuolumne Band of Me-Wuk Indians
nations.lands: Sierra Nevada foothills, Tuolumne County, California

facts.text: In January 2005 the Tribe opened the Tuolumne Me-Wuk Indian Health Center.

source.title: History - The Tuolumne Band of Me-Wuk Indians

facts.text: Tuolumne Rancheria began in 1910 with 289.52 acres; today the Tribe holds more than 1,700 acres of fee and trust land.

source.title: History - The Tuolumne Band of Me-Wuk Indians

nations.name: Swinomish Indian Tribal Community
nations.lands: Swinomish Reservation near La Conner, Skagit County, Washington

facts.text: The Swinomish Tribe monitors air quality in partnership with the EPA, with two major oil refineries right next to its reservation.
Swinomish monitors record real-time data on particulates, ozone and nitrogen dioxide, plus weather such as wind, temperature, humidity and precipitation.

nations.name: Wounaan
nations.lands: Darién and eastern Panama, including the Emberá-Wounaan comarca and collective lands, and the San Juan River region of Colombia

facts.text: Wounaan forest technicians map illegal clearing with smartphone apps and GIS, and communities bring that evidence to the Wounaan National Congress.

source.title: Panama's Indigenous Groups Wage High-Tech Fight for Their Lands
source.publisher: Yale Environment 360, Yale School of the Environment

facts.text: Panama's 2023 census counted 10,634 Wounaan people.

source.title: Cuadro 20. Población indígena en la República, por sexo, según provincia, comarca indígena, grupo indígena al que pertenece y grupos de edad: Censo 2023
source.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censo (INEC), Panama

nations.name: K'iche'
nations.lands: Western highlands of Guatemala, including Quiché, Totonicapán, Quetzaltenango and Sololá

facts.text: In Totonicapán, the 48 Cantones is a K'iche' ancestral authority built from community governments, with representatives chosen each year in assembly.

source.title: Former Indigenous authorities of the 48 Cantones of Totonicapán released in Guatemala after more than a year in pretrial detention

facts.text: The 48 Cantones' system of caring for forests and water has served as an example for communities all over Guatemala.

nations.name: Q'eqchi'
nations.lands: Alta Verapaz, Izabal and Petén in Guatemala, and the Toledo District of southern Belize

facts.text: Radio Chiquixji in Alta Verapaz, Guatemala, broadcasts for bilingual Q'eqchi' and Spanish speakers and for communities that speak only Q'eqchi'.

source.title: Announcing Our 2019 Community Media Grants Partners

facts.text: In southern Belize, 39 Q'eqchi' and Mopan Maya communities have rights to their customary lands, as Belize's highest appeals court affirmed in 2015.

source.title: Maya Leaders Alliance Advocates at United Nations Urging Respect for Rule of Law in Belize

nations.name: Cabécar
nations.lands: Indigenous territories in the Talamanca mountains and Chirripó area of Costa Rica, in Limón, Cartago and Puntarenas provinces

facts.text: Costa Rica's 2011 census found that 87.6 percent of people in the official Cabécar territories speak the Cabécar language.
Costa Rica's 2013 list of Indigenous territories includes Cabécar territories such as Alto Chirripó, Bajo Chirripó, Talamanca Cabécar, Ujarrás and Telire.

source.title: Anexo 6: Pueblos y territorios indígenas de Costa Rica (2013)

nations.name: Buglé
nations.lands: The Ngäbe-Buglé comarca and nearby areas of Bocas del Toro and Veraguas in western Panama

facts.text: Under Panama's 1997 comarca law, the comarca's General Congress is the highest body for the ethnic and cultural voice and decisions of the Ngäbe-Buglé people.

source.title: Ley 10 de 7 de marzo de 1997, por la cual se crea la Comarca Ngöbe-Buglé
source.publisher: FAOLEX, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

facts.text: Panama's 2023 census counted 23,898 Buglé people; about 12,000 of them live in the Ngäbe-Buglé comarca, which they share with the Ngäbe.

source.title: Cuadro 20. Población indígena en la República, por sexo, según provincia, comarca indígena, grupo indígena al que pertenece y grupos de edad: Censo 2023
source.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censo (INEC), Panama

nations.name: Naso Tjër Di
nations.lands: The Naso Tjër Di comarca along the Teribe River in Bocas del Toro, northwestern Panama, near the Costa Rican border

facts.text: The Naso are led by a king who lives in Sieyik, where Panama's president came in 2020 to sign the law creating their comarca.

source.title: Indigenous community wins recognition of its land rights in Panama

facts.text: In December 2020 Panama created the 1,600 square kilometer Naso Tjër Di comarca, the result of decades of Naso efforts to secure their land rights.

source.title: Indigenous community wins recognition of its land rights in Panama

nations.name: Mopan
nations.lands: The Toledo District of southern Belize and nearby Petén, Guatemala

facts.text: In 2022 a Free, Prior and Informed Consultation Protocol for the Maya of southern Belize was adopted, and in 2025 a working draft on protecting Maya customary land tenure followed.

source.title: Closing Remarks at the Final Monitoring Hearing in Maya Leaders v The Attorney General of Belize [2015] CCJ 15 (AJ)

facts.text: A 2015 Caribbean Court of Justice judgment obliges Belize's government to mark out and register Maya village lands in the south and guard them against outsiders.

source.title: Maya Q'eqchi and Mopan of Southern Belize Win Major Land Rights Victory in International Appeals Court (statement by the Maya Leaders Alliance)

nations.name: Miskitu
nations.lands: The Caribbean coast of Nicaragua and La Moskitia in northeastern Honduras, along the Wangki (Coco) River

facts.text: In 2021 the Yapti Tasba community radio network, linked to Miskitu organization YATAMA, reached 17 Indigenous territories and 154 communities, 95 percent of them Miskitu.

source.title: Pueblo Miskitu, YATAMA, and Yapti Tasba Radios Advance Indigenous Rights on the North Caribbean Coast of Nicaragua

facts.text: Nicaragua's Caribbean Coast autonomy law affirms that Indigenous communities there have the right to keep and develop their languages and to bilingual education.

source.title: Pueblo Miskitu, YATAMA, and Yapti Tasba Radios Advance Indigenous Rights on the North Caribbean Coast of Nicaragua

nations.name: Garifuna
nations.lands: Caribbean coast of Honduras, Belize, Guatemala and Nicaragua, plus large diaspora communities

facts.text: In 2024, Belize observed Garifuna Settlement Day on 19 November as one of its official public holidays.
Most Garifuna communities today are in Honduras, Guatemala, Nicaragua and Belize, and the Garifuna language is part of the Arawakan family.

source.title: Language, dance and music of the Garifuna

nations.name: Kalinago
nations.lands: The Kalinago Territory on the northeast coast of Dominica, in the eastern Caribbean

facts.text: In July 2024, voters in the Kalinago Territory elected their Kalinago Chief; the winning candidate received about 58 percent of the votes counted.
The Kalinago Territory has its own local government: a Chief and six councillors elected by residents every five years, alongside representation in Dominica's parliament.

source.title: The Kalinago Territory
source.publisher: Division of Culture, Government of the Commonwealth of Dominica

nations.name: Mayangna
nations.lands: The Bosawás region and North Caribbean Coast of Nicaragua, with related Tawahka communities in Honduras

facts.text: After the 2020 hurricanes, Mayangna communities in Bonanza rebuilt together: they repaired 15 roofs collectively and planted 50 plots of grains, beans, corn and cassava.

source.title: Mayagna Communities Work to Achieve Food Sovereignty after Hurricanes Iota and Eta

facts.text: Nicaragua's Bosawás Biosphere Reserve, in the Mosquitia region, is ancestral territory of the Mayangna and Miskitu peoples, whose rights there are recognized.

source.title: Indigenous, Garifuna, and Feminist Community Correspondents Push for a More Inclusive Democracy

source.title: Alegres le abrimos las puertas de nuestra casa, como usted nos ha abierto las puertas del Palacio, dice el pueblo xinca al presidente Arévalo

source.title: Huaves : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura

nations.lands: Southern Veracruz, Mexico, in the Isthmus region, including Soteapan and Sayula

source.title: Popolucas : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura

nations.lands: La Cañada region of northeastern Oaxaca, Mexico, including Cuicatlán, Concepción Pápalo and Santos Reyes Pápalo

source.title: Cuicatecos : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura

nations.name: Kankuamo
nations.lands: South-eastern foothills of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta near Valledupar, Cesar, Colombia, centered on Atánquez

facts.text: The Kankuamo resguardo, about 24,212 hectares near Valledupar, was collectively titled to the people in 2003.

source.title: Kankuamos, guardianes del equilibrio del mundo
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

facts.text: In 2022 UNESCO recognized the ancestral knowledge system shared by the Kankuamo, Arhuaco, Kogui and Wiwa as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

nations.name: Mapuche
nations.lands: South-central Chile, especially La Araucanía and Santiago, and Patagonian provinces of Argentina such as Neuquén and Río Negro

facts.text: Most Mapuche in Chile today live in cities, with the largest groups in La Araucanía region and in the capital, Santiago.
Mapudungun, the Mapuche language, is still the most widely spoken Indigenous language in Chile.

nations.name: Uru Chipaya
nations.lands: Chipaya, on the altiplano of Oruro department, Bolivia

facts.text: The Uru Chipaya nation approved its own autonomy statute by referendum in 2016 and in 2017 became one of Bolivia's first three Indigenous self-governments.

source.title: Charagua, Raqaypampa y Uru Chipaya conforman los primeros tres autogobiernos indígenas de Bolivia
source.publisher: Órgano Electoral Plurinacional de Bolivia, Fuente Directa

facts.text: Leadership of the Uru Chipaya executive rotates in turns among the nation's four ayllus: Aranzaya, Manazaya, Wistrullani and Ayparavi.

source.title: La rotación de ayllus en el Lanqsñi Paqh mä eph (Órgano Ejecutivo)
source.publisher: Órgano Electoral Plurinacional de Bolivia, Fuente Directa

nations.name: Arhuaco
nations.lands: South-eastern slopes of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta in Cesar and Magdalena, northern Colombia

facts.text: The Confederación Indígena Tayrona, the Arhuaco organization founded in 1976, plans to restore the Guatapurí river basin with 18,000 native trees.
In 2022 UNESCO inscribed the ancestral knowledge system of the Arhuaco, Kankuamo, Kogui and Wiwa peoples as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

nations.name: Kichwa Saraguro
nations.lands: Saraguro canton in Loja province and nearby areas of southern Ecuador

facts.text: In 2019 Radio Kipa, a new community radio station in Saraguro, was one of the few radios to have won a license from Ecuador's state in recent years, and planned to train 30 young people.

source.title: Announcing Our 2019 Community Media Grants Partners

facts.text: CORPUKIS, a coordinating body of Kichwa Saraguro organizations, works with grassroots groups to advance civil, human and collective rights in its territory.

source.title: Announcing Our 2019 Community Media Grants Partners

nations.name: Lickanantay
nations.lands: Oases and valleys of the Salar de Atacama and the Loa river basin, Antofagasta Region, northern Chile

facts.text: Lickanantay communities are revitalizing their language, Ckunsa. A 2025 regional arts project in Chiu Chiu promotes it through art and stop-motion animation.

source.title: Proyecto Fondart Regional 2025 impulsa la revitalización de la lengua Ckunsa a través del arte y la animación en Chiu Chiu
source.publisher: Ministerio de las Culturas, las Artes y el Patrimonio de Chile

facts.text: Lickanantay communities live in the oases and valleys of the Atacama salt flat and the Loa river basin in Chile's Antofagasta Region.

nations.name: Pasto
nations.lands: Highlands of Nariño, Colombia, in municipalities such as Cumbal, Guachucal, Ipiales and Túquerres, and across the border in northern Ecuador

facts.text: The Pasto are working to recover their identity, oral tradition and ancestral customs, and to strengthen their own law through their cabildos.

source.title: Pastos, los hijos del sol
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

facts.text: Most Pasto communities live in resguardos dating from colonial times and in other lands in Nariño, such as Cumbal, Guachucal, Ipiales and Túquerres.

source.title: Pastos, los hijos del sol
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

nations.name: Uro
nations.lands: Lake Titicaca, especially the Bay of Puno in Peru, with Uru communities also in Bolivia

facts.text: Uro communities today are working to recover knowledge of their ancestral language, with support from Peru's Ministry of Culture.

source.title: Uro | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

facts.text: For centuries the Uro have lived on large rafts of totora reed, called floating islands, on Lake Titicaca in the Bay of Puno, and many Uro families still live on them.

source.title: Uro | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

nations.name: Kichwa
nations.lands: Highland provinces of Ecuador along the Andes, from Imbabura and Pichincha south to Chimborazo, Cañar and Loja

facts.text: Ecuador's Constitution names Kichwa, together with Spanish and Shuar, as official languages of intercultural relations.

source.title: Constitución de la República traducida al kichwa

facts.text: In 2009 Ecuador's Constitution was translated into Kichwa, with five delegates from Indigenous communities reviewing the translation.

source.title: Constitución de la República traducida al kichwa

nations.name: Colla
nations.lands: Atacama Region of Chile, around Copiapó, Chañaral, Tierra Amarilla and Diego de Almagro, and the puna of northwestern Argentina

facts.text: The first Colla Indigenous communities in Chile were officially constituted in the early 1990s.
Colla communities in Chile are found in Atacama Region areas such as Potrerillos and Inca de Oro, in Chañaral, Copiapó and Tierra Amarilla.

nations.name: Yanacona
nations.lands: The Macizo Colombiano in southern Cauca, with communities in Huila and Valle del Cauca, Colombia

facts.text: The Yanacona are recovering their identity and culture, including their traditional language, Quechua, and strengthening their cabildo authorities.

source.title: Los Yanacona, reconstruyendo la casa
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

facts.text: Yanacona territory covers a large part of the Macizo Colombiano, the mountain region of southern Cauca.

source.title: Los Yanacona, reconstruyendo la casa
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

nations.name: Ahtna
nations.lands: Copper River basin and the upper Susitna and Nenana river areas, Alaska, United States

source.title: Languages - Ahtna
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

facts.text: Ahtna is the Athabascan language of the Copper River and the upper Susitna and Nenana drainages, home to eight Ahtna communities.

source.title: Languages - Ahtna
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Cup'ik
nations.lands: Chevak and the nearby Bering Sea coast of southwest Alaska, United States

facts.text: In Chevak the people and their language are called Cup'ik, and on Nunivak Island the related form is Cup'ig, each used in place of the word Yup'ik.

source.title: Languages - Central Yup'ik
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

facts.text: Hooper Bay-Chevak is one of the five dialects of the Central Alaskan Yup'ik language.

source.title: Languages - Central Yup'ik
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Dena'ina
nations.lands: Cook Inlet region of Southcentral Alaska, including the Kenai Peninsula and the Anchorage area, United States

facts.text: The Kenaitze Indian Tribe states its vision as assuring that the Kahtnuht'ana Dena'ina thrive forever.
Dena'ina is the only Alaska Athabascan language spoken in a coastal setting, and the only one spoken on both sides of the Alaska Range.

source.title: Languages - Dena'ina
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Hän
nations.lands: Eagle, Alaska, United States, and Dawson, Yukon, Canada, along the upper Yukon River

facts.text: Hän is one of ten Doyon region languages for which Doyon Languages Online is creating introductory online lessons.
The Hän language is spoken at Eagle in Alaska and at Dawson in Yukon, and language centers on both sides of the border have documented it.

source.title: Languages - Hän
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Koyukon
nations.lands: Villages along the Koyukuk River and the middle Yukon River, Interior Alaska, United States

facts.text: Doyon Languages Online is creating introductory online lessons for Denaakk'e and nine other Doyon region languages; its first courses came out in summer 2019 and are free.
The language name Denaakk'e comes from denaa, meaning people, plus a suffix meaning like, so it literally means like us.

source.title: Languages - Koyukon
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Tlingit
nations.lands: Coastal Southeast Alaska from Yakutat south to Ketchikan, United States, with citizens living worldwide

facts.text: The Central Council of the Tlingit and Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska is the tribal government for more than 38,000 Tlingit and Haida citizens worldwide.

source.title: Central Council of the Tlingit & Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska
source.publisher: Central Council of the Tlingit & Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska

facts.text: Sealaska Heritage Institute says young people who learned Lingít and other Southeast Alaska languages, once nearly lost to oppression, now teach them with help from fluent Elders.

nations.name: Alutiiq/Sugpiaq
nations.lands: Kodiak Archipelago, Alaska Peninsula, outer Kenai Peninsula and Prince William Sound, Alaska, United States

facts.text: At the Alutiiq Museum, fluent speakers, learners and linguists work together to record Sugt'stun and teach it to a new generation of speakers.
Sugpiaq, the people's traditional name for themselves, joins suk, meaning person, with piaq, meaning real.

source.title: Languages - Alutiiq / Sugpiaq
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: CHamoru
nations.lands: Guam (Guåhan) in the Mariana Islands, a United States territory

facts.text: Guam's Department of Chamorro Affairs works to preserve, develop and promote CHamoru heritage, with a division devoted to language and culture.

source.title: About Us
source.publisher: Department of Chamorro Affairs, Government of Guam

facts.text: Guam's Public Law 12-132 made both English and CHamoru official languages of the island.

source.title: Role of Education in the Preservation of Guam's Indigenous Language

nations.name: Native Hawaiians
nations.lands: The Hawaiian Islands (Hawaiʻi), United States

facts.text: The Office of Hawaiian Affairs, approved by Hawaiʻi voters in 1978 to serve Native Hawaiians, is governed by nine trustees elected statewide for four-year terms.
Since a 1978 amendment to the state constitution, Hawaiian and English have both been official languages of the State of Hawaiʻi.

source.title: State Constitution
source.publisher: Legislative Reference Bureau, State of Hawaiʻi

nations.name: Eyak
nations.lands: Cordova, the Copper River Delta and Prince William Sound, Alaska, United States

facts.text: The Native Village of Eyak in Cordova is a federally recognized tribe that unites Eyak, Chugach Region, Tlingit and Athabaskan peoples.

source.title: Native Village of Eyak - About Us

facts.text: Eyak is not an Athabascan language but its own branch beside the Athabascan languages, within the Athabascan-Eyak-Tlingit language family.

source.title: Languages - Eyak
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Yup'ik
nations.lands: Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta and nearby coasts and rivers of southwest Alaska, United States

facts.text: In the Calista Region along the Yukon and Kuskokwim rivers, subsistence hunting, fishing and gathering bind communities together and are part of who people are.
The word Yup'ik names both the language and the people, built from yuk, meaning person, and pik, meaning real.

source.title: Languages - Central Yup'ik
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Mansi
nations.lands: Ob and Irtysh basin in western Siberia, mainly Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug (Yugra), with small groups in Yamal-Nenets Autonomous Okrug and Sverdlovsk Oblast, Russia

facts.text: Luima Seripos, a newspaper in the Mansi language, first came out on 11 February 1989 and is still produced today in a joint newsroom with the Khanty paper.

source.title: Историческая справка
source.publisher: Khanty Mansi Mir (joint editorial office of the Khanty Yasang and Luima Seripos newspapers)

facts.text: Mansi rapper Yevgeny Anyamov, known as Bizzo, records his songs in Mansi and opened his own studio in his hometown of Ivdel to share his people's culture with youth.

nations.name: Nivkh
nations.lands: Lower Amur River in Khabarovsk Krai and Sakhalin Island, Russia

facts.text: The Nivkh speak a language isolate, probably one of the oldest languages of Eurasia. Its links to other languages have not been established.

source.title: Нивхи
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: Nivkh life was built on fishing and hunting, including sea mammals taken with spears or with nets woven from leather straps.

source.title: Нивхи
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Luoravetlan
nations.lands: Chukotka Autonomous Okrug, northern Kamchatka Krai and the Nizhnekolymsky District of Sakha (Yakutia), Russia

facts.text: Researchers at Russia's Kunstkamera museum published a 2018 study on the mobile dwellings of Chukchi reindeer herders, covering both traditions and innovations.

source.title: Arctic Research Center
source.publisher: Peter the Great Museum of Anthropology and Ethnography (Kunstkamera), Russian Academy of Sciences

facts.text: Carving bone and walrus ivory and embroidering with reindeer hair are long-standing Chukchi arts, practised alongside reindeer herding and hunting.

source.title: Чукчи
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Even
nations.lands: Northeastern Siberia: Sakha (Yakutia), Magadan Oblast, Kamchatka, Chukotka and Khabarovsk Krai, Russia

facts.text: The Even language belongs to the Tungusic (Manchu-Tungus) branch and is close to Evenki. Even self-names include Even (local) and Orochel (reindeer people).

source.title: Эвены
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: The 2002 census counted 11,657 Even living in the Republic of Sakha (Yakutia).

source.title: Эвены
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Itelmen
nations.lands: Tigilsky District on the west coast of Kamchatka Krai, with smaller groups in Chukotka and Magadan Oblast, Russia

facts.text: Western Itelmen is the Itelmen language that has been kept to the present day.

source.title: Ительмены
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: Fishing, above all for salmon, is the traditional Itelmen livelihood on Kamchatka.

source.title: Ительмены
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Ket
nations.lands: Yenisei River basin, mainly Turukhansky District of Krasnoyarsk Krai, Russia

facts.text: A Cyrillic writing system that Ket speakers actually use came into being in the late 1980s.

source.title: Кеты
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: Ket is the only living language of the Yeniseian language family.

source.title: Кеты
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Inughuit
nations.lands: Avanersuaq (the Thule region) in northwest Greenland, centred on the town of Qaanaaq

facts.text: Hunting is still a significant part of the livelihood of several families in Qaanaaq, Greenland's youngest and northernmost town.
The Inughuit have their own language, or dialect, and a hunting culture that is distinctive in several ways.

nations.name: Yupik
nations.lands: Settlements on the eastern coast of the Chukchi Peninsula, Chukotka Autonomous Okrug, Russia, across the Bering Strait from Alaska

facts.text: Inuit from Chukotka became part of the Inuit Circumpolar Council in 1992, a goal that was in ICC's vision from the very beginning.
Yupik hunters are regarded as originators of traditional whaling in the region, hunting walrus, seal and whale with harpoons.

source.title: Эскимосы
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Evenki
nations.lands: Siberian taiga from the Ob River to the Sea of Okhotsk, with the largest group in Sakha (Yakutia), also Krasnoyarsk and Khabarovsk krais, Buryatia, Amur, Irkutsk and Zabaykalsky regions of Russia, and in China and Mongolia

facts.text: Evenki communities live across Russia, with the largest in Sakha (Yakutia), and Evenki also live in China and Mongolia.

source.title: Эвенки
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: Evenki homelands span a huge part of the Siberian taiga, from the Ob River in the west to the Sea of Okhotsk in the east.

source.title: The Evenks
source.publisher: The Red Book of the Peoples of the Russian Empire (Institute of the Estonian Language archive)

nations.name: Dolgan
nations.lands: Taimyr Peninsula in Krasnoyarsk Krai (Taimyr Dolgan-Nenets District) and the Anabar District and city of Yakutsk in Sakha (Yakutia), Russia

facts.text: During an August 2026 folk culture expedition to Khatanga, the Dolgan dried-fish dish kerdiileek was added to the list of Taimyr's intangible cultural heritage.

source.title: Долганская юкола «кэрдиилээк» признана объектом нематериального наследия Таймыра
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: Dolgan is a Turkic language, close to Sakha (Yakut), from which it separated through isolated development.

source.title: Долганы
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Wajãpi
nations.lands: Wajãpi Indigenous Land in Amapá, Brazil, and the middle and upper Oyapock River in French Guiana

facts.text: In 1994 the Wajãpi began demarcating their own Indigenous Land in Amapá, Brazil, and founded the Council of Wajãpi Villages, known as Apina.

source.title: Wajãpi
source.publisher: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil

facts.text: In French Guiana the Wayãpi live along the middle and upper Oyapock River.

nations.name: Wayana
nations.lands: Upper Maroni River and its tributaries in French Guiana, the Tapanahony and Paloemeu rivers in Suriname, and the East Paru River in Pará, Brazil

facts.text: France recognizes Wayana as one of six Amerindian languages of French Guiana with the status of a language of France.

source.title: Langues de France et langues régionales en Guyane: bilan au 7 décembre 2015
source.publisher: Ministère de la Culture, Direction des affaires culturelles de Guyane

facts.text: Among younger people on Brazil's East Paru River, the Wayana language has gained great prestige.

source.title: Wayana
source.publisher: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil

nations.name: Uwottüja
nations.lands: The Autana, Cuao, Sipapo and Guayapo rivers and the middle Orinoco, Amazonas state, Venezuela

facts.text: In 2020 Uwottüja communities of the Autana, Cuao, Sipapo and Guayapo rivers met at Pendare and declared themselves guardians of their territory.

source.title: Pronunciamiento del Pueblo Indígena Uwottüja de los habitantes de los cuatro ríos Autana, Cuao, Sipapo, Guayapo y el sector Orinoco Medio
source.publisher: Pueblo Indígena Uwottüja, published by the Observatorio de Ecología Política de Venezuela

facts.text: The Uwottüja held their first congress as a people in 1984, uniting around the defense of their ancestral lands 'like one churuata, with one voice'.

source.title: Pronunciamiento del Pueblo Indígena Uwottüja de los habitantes de los cuatro ríos Autana, Cuao, Sipapo, Guayapo y el sector Orinoco Medio
source.publisher: Pueblo Indígena Uwottüja, published by the Observatorio de Ecología Política de Venezuela

nations.name: Ye'kwana
nations.lands: Amazonas and Bolívar states in southern Venezuela, and the Auaris and Uraricoera rivers of Roraima, Brazil

facts.text: The name Ye'kwana, which the people use for themselves, entered Venezuela's census in 1982 and has almost fully replaced the outside name Makiritare.

source.title: Censo Nacional de Población y Vivienda 2011: Empadronamiento de la Población Indígena

facts.text: Among themselves the Ye'kwana use So'to, meaning 'people', while Ye'kwana can be translated as 'canoe people'.

source.title: Ye'kwana
source.publisher: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil

nations.name: Teko
nations.lands: Camopi on the Oyapock River and Cayodé on the upper Maroni, French Guiana

facts.text: France lists Teko, formerly called Émerillon, among French Guiana's six Amerindian languages recognized as languages of France.

source.title: Langues de France et langues régionales en Guyane: bilan au 7 décembre 2015
source.publisher: Ministère de la Culture, Direction des affaires culturelles de Guyane

facts.text: Teko and Wayãpi are the two Tupi-Guarani languages spoken in the Amazonian Park of French Guiana, where Wayana belongs to the Carib family.

nations.name: Pemón
nations.lands: Savannas of southeastern Venezuela, the Kamarang River area of Guyana, and Roraima state in Brazil

facts.text: Taurepang, Arekuna and Kamarakoto communities share the self-name Pemon, a word meaning 'people' or 'us'.

source.title: Taurepang
source.publisher: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil

facts.text: In Guyana, Arekuna communities live on the banks of the Kamarang River.

source.title: Indigenous Nations
source.publisher: Ministry of Amerindian Affairs, Government of Guyana

nations.name: Akawaio
nations.lands: Upper Mazaruni area and nearby river valleys of western Guyana, with Akawaio also counted in Venezuela's census

facts.text: Akawaio is one of the nine Indigenous languages covered by Guyana's language revival programme, which the government moved to restart in 2021.

source.title: Gov't to resume Amerindian language revival project
source.publisher: Department of Public Information, Government of Guyana

facts.text: Kapohn is the Akawaio people's own name for themselves, and like most peoples of Guyana's interior they are Carib speakers.

nations.name: Barí
nations.lands: Serranía de los Motilones and the Catatumbo and Oro river basins in Norte de Santander, Colombia, and Zulia state, Venezuela

facts.text: The Barí language, of the Chibcha family, is being passed on to new generations and has speakers of all ages.
Barí live in the foothills of Colombia's Serranía de los Motilones along the Catatumbo and Oro rivers, with settlements also in Zulia state, Venezuela.
